1.title: Parts of Speech
learn: Identify how a word functions in context, not only how it looks.
Recognise common, proper, countable, uncountable, collective and compound nouns.
Distinguish main, auxiliary, modal, transitive and intransitive verbs.
Notice what each word modifies and the information it adds.
Separate reference words from words that introduce or specify nouns.
Recognise relationship words and linking words.
examples: I work every day. / My work is demanding.
That book is mine. / I know that you’re busy.
strategy: Decide the word class from its function in the sentence.
Expect the same word form to belong to different classes in different contexts.
Use the words around the target word as evidence.

2.title: Grammatical Structures
learn: Actions in progress and temporary situations.
Past actions connected to the present.
Meaning expressed through modal verbs and future forms.
How form changes when focus or reporting changes.
examples: She has lived here for five years.
He said that he was tired.
strategy: Look for time reference and communicative meaning before naming the tense.
Separate form from use: the same structure can carry different meanings.
Pay attention to auxiliaries because they often reveal the structure.

3.title: Lexis: Meaning & Word Formation
learn: Prefixes and suffixes change meaning or word class.
Recognise the core form from which related words are built.
Two or more words can combine into one lexical unit.
Words may share a root but belong to different word classes.
Meaning may not be predictable from the individual words.
Verb + particle combinations often create a distinct meaning.
strategy: Use morphology as a clue, but always confirm meaning from context.
Treat idioms and phrasal verbs as lexical units.
Notice whether the question asks about form, meaning or relationship.

4.title: Lexical Relationships & Register
learn: Words with the same or very similar meaning.
Words grouped by topic or semantic field.
Words with the same pronunciation but different spelling/meaning.
Language choices shaped by formality, relationship and context.
examples: make a decision / heavy rain / take an exam
Could you possibly…? vs Can you…?
strategy: For collocation, choose what sounds conventionally natural, not merely grammatical.
For register, identify audience, relationship and situation.
Do not confuse lexical set with synonymy.

5.title: Phonology: Sounds & Stress
learn: Different sound categories in spoken English.
Some consonants are voiced; others are unvoiced.
Two words differing in one phoneme.
One syllable is more prominent in a word.
Prominent words carry key meaning or contrast.
strategy: Think in sounds, not spelling.
Use minimal pairs to identify exactly which sound changes.
For stress questions, listen for prominence rather than syllable length alone.

6.title: Phonology: Intonation & Connected Speech
learn: Pitch movement can signal attitude and discourse meaning.
Natural speech flows as a continuous stream.
Function words often reduce in unstressed positions.
Sounds may disappear in rapid connected speech.
strategy: Do not analyse connected speech as isolated dictionary words.
Look for reduced function words and sound links.
Remember that intonation can change speaker attitude without changing grammar.

7.title: Functions
learn: Asking someone to join or attend.
examples: Would you like to join us?
I’m afraid I won’t be able to come.
strategy: Identify what the speaker is doing, not just the grammar used.
Check formality and appropriacy for the situation.
Different exponents can express the same function.

8.title: Language Skills & Subskills
learn: Listen for gist, detail, attitude or prediction.
examples: Read quickly for the main idea.
Find a departure time in a timetable.
Check spelling and grammar in a final draft.
strategy: Match the subskill to the learner’s immediate purpose.
Do not confuse editing with proofreading.
Gist and detail tasks require different reading/listening behaviour.

9.title: Motivation, Exposure & Acquisition
learn: Reasons and energy for learning can change over time.
Contact with the target language inside and outside class.
Language can develop gradually through meaningful use.
Comprehension may develop before much production.
Communication creates opportunities to negotiate meaning.
Brief attention to language features within meaningful communication.
examples: Pause briefly to notice a useful grammar pattern.
strategy: Exposure alone is not the whole story: interaction and attention to form also matter.
Treat motivation as dynamic, not fixed.
Distinguish acquisition processes from explicit study.

10.title: Errors & L1/L2 Learning
learn: A slip can often be self-corrected; an error reflects incomplete learning.
A normal stage in building the L2 system.
A rule is applied too widely.
Some errors become persistent over time.
examples: Word order transferred from the first language.
strategy: Ask whether the learner could self-correct before deciding slip vs error.
Errors can be useful diagnostic evidence.
Correction timing should fit the activity aim.

11.title: Learners: Characteristics & Needs
learn: Development can influence attention, confidence and classroom behaviour.
L1/L2 environments differ in exposure and use.
Learners may prefer different modes and interaction patterns.
Learners use deliberate techniques to support learning.
Previous classes can shape confidence and expectations.
Personal, academic and professional goals influence priorities.
examples: A learner expects grammar translation because previous courses used it.
strategy: Do not treat preferences as fixed learner types.
Distinguish needs from preferences.
Use learner profiles to explain teaching choices.

12.title: Presenting Language
learn: A short activity that energises or settles learners.
Helps people get to know one another.
Creates interest and activates knowledge for the main topic.
Puts language into a meaningful situation.
Confirms that learners understand the target meaning.
examples: Discuss travel before a reading about tourism.
Present “I’d like…” in a restaurant scene.
Do I still live here now?
strategy: Separate warmer, ice-breaker and lead-in by their main aim.
A strong presentation connects meaning, form and pronunciation.
Use focused CCQs instead of only asking “Do you understand?”

13.title: Teaching Activities & Techniques
learn: Guided oral practice based on a model.
Get learners to supply language or information.
Give a clue to support learner production.
Use techniques that support accuracy and independence.
examples: I bought a book. Pen → I bought a pen.
strategy: Identify the teacher’s immediate aim behind the technique.
Control refers mainly to how much language choice learners have.
Different correction techniques shift responsibility between teacher and learner.

14.title: Teaching Approaches & Lesson Frameworks
learn: Meaningful task first, then language focus.
Learners infer rules from examples with support.
examples: Plan a trip → discuss language used.
strategy: Identify the sequence first; the sequence often reveals the framework.
Separate a teaching technique from a complete lesson framework.
Look for what is central: target language, task, discovery, physical response, translation, chunks or skills.

15.title: Assessment
learn: Level placement vs identifying strengths and weaknesses.
Learning during a course vs attainment over a completed programme.
Ability independent of one specific taught course.
Self, peer, portfolio, formal, informal and continuous assessment.
examples: Which level class should this learner join?
What does this learner need to work on?
Feedback on a draft before final submission.
strategy: Classify assessment mainly by its purpose.
A task format can serve different purposes depending on how results are used.
Distinguish assessment purpose from assessment method.
